identity.author: John Davenant
identity.work: Two Dissertations (De praedestinatione through Cap. X Ultimum Secunda)
identity.edition: Dissertationes duae (Cambridge: Roger Daniel, 1650). Partial through Cap. X Ultimum triple-cord Major. Further Cap. X remains.

scope.locus: De praedestinatione Cap. X Ultimum Secunda cont. (De bono pers. 23; Vasquez; Patres; triple-cord).
scope.next_locus: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 1 (Orthodox Grace of Christ vs Pelagius: illuminating/exciting vs healing/regenerating; then Arminius parallel).

sections.title: Cap. X Ultimum Secunda: true grace not according to merits cannot stand without predestination without antecedent regard to merits — Aug. De bono pers. 23
english: Hence, because God’s true grace—not given according to merits—cannot stand unless predestination also is laid down without antecedent regard to merits, Augustine did not hesitate to affirm (De bono perseverantiae 23) that the Church of Christ never lacked the faith of this predestination now defended with fresh care against new heretics. As if to say: every catholic who admitted that vivifying, saving grace is given or withheld according to God’s purpose of mercy or non-mercy, even if they never named election and preterition, yet because of the knot binding the things themselves sensed the same about predestination.
sections.latin: Et hinc, quia vera Dei gratia, quae non datur secundum merita, haud potest consistere nisi praedestinatio etiam absque antecedaneo intuitu ad merita ponatur, non dubitavit Augustinus affirmare, Praedestinationis hujus fidem, quae contra novos haereticos nova sollicitudine nunc defenditur, nunquam Ecclesiam Christi non habuisse, De bono persever. cap. 23. quasi dixisset, Catholicos omnes qui admiserunt gratiam vivificam et salutiferam dari et non dari secundum propositum Dei miserentis aut non miserentis, etiamsi de electione et praeteritione nullum verbum fecerint, tamen propter ipsarum rerum inter se connexionem eodem etiam modo de praedestinatione sensisse.

sections.title: Cap. X Ultimum Secunda: Vasquez — Pelagians spoke the same way of predestination and of grace; God gives in time as he disposed from eternity
english: Lest resting on Augustine alone seem unfair, hear Vasquez the Jesuit on the knot of these questions (In 1. Aquin. disp. 91, c. 2, p. 631): The Pelagians, he says, spoke the same way of Predestination and of Grace; of old the same question of Grace and Predestination stood between Pelagius and the catholics. The reason is ready: God gives his grace in time as he disposed to give it from eternity. If from eternity he predestined saving grace to be given freely to someone, then in time he gives it freely; and if in time he gives only with regard to some prior good act of the human will, then from eternity he predestined that he would not give otherwise.
sections.latin: Sed ne cuiquam videatur paulo iniquius, si solius Augustini judicio acquiescamus, audite quid Vasquez Jesuitae de connexione harum quaestionum fateatur, In 1. Aquin. disp. 91. cap. 2. pag. 631. Pelagiani eodem modo, inquit, de Praedestinatione et de Gratia loquebantur: eadem etiam fuit antiquitus quaestio de Gratia et de Praedestinatione inter Pelagium et Catholicos. Hujusce rei ratio in promptu: Nam Deus eodem modo donat gratiam suam in tempore, quo disposuit illam donare ab aeterno. Si ab aeterno praedestinavit gratiam salutiferam gratuito dandam alicui, tum in tempore dat eam gratuito: et e contra, si in tempore non dat nisi ex intuitu ad praeviam aliquam bonam operationem voluntatis humanae, tum ab aeterno praedestinavit se non aliter daturum.

sections.title: Cap. X Ultimum Secunda: who deny opposite human merits as causes why saving grace is given or withheld are held to deny that foresight difference as distinguishing conditions of election
english: Deny that opposite merits and demerits of human wills—good acts in some, evil in others—are why saving grace is given here and withheld there, and you are held, by that same denial, to deny that the foreseen difference among those wills was, for election, predestination, and preterition, a cause or occasion or distinguishing condition.
sections.latin: Qui igitur negant opposita humanarum voluntatum merita et demerita, id est, bonos actus horum, malos illorum, esse causas cur gratia salutifera hisce detur, illis non detur, eadem opera negasse putentur praevisam hanc humanarum voluntatum differentiam fuisse electionis, praedestinationis, et praeteritionis sive causas, sive occasiones, sive conditiones distinguentes.

sections.title: Cap. X Ultimum Ultimo: Fathers before Pelagius need mild reading — election referred to foresight of merits means execution, not intention (Suarez)
english: Last join this: the Fathers who spoke more freely before Pelagius arose need mild reading in many places. They sometimes refer election to foresight of merits—but election there is to be taken not as intention but as execution, as Suarez notes not amiss (Opusc. lib. 3, De auxiliis Divinae gratiae 18). And often they draw that very foresight of merits in the elect from no first fountain but the gratuitous will of God predestinating.
sections.latin: Ultimo et illud jungendum, Patres illos qui ante exortum Pelagium securius loquebantur, in multis benigna interpretatione indigere. Referunt illi nonnunquam electionem ad praescientiam meritorum: sed de electione intelligendi sunt non per modum intentionis, sed per modum exsecutionis accepta, ut haud incommode annotavit Suarez, Opusc. lib. 3, De auxil. Divin. grat. cap. 18. Porro, saepenumero hanc ipsam praescientiam meritorum in electis non aliunde quam ex Dei praedestinantis gratuita voluntate ex primo fonte deducunt.

sections.title: Cap. X Ultimum: Chrysostom sometimes overstates free will, yet elsewhere grace alone; Orthodox ‘preparing for grace’ means exciting grace leads on to justification
english: Chrysostom sometimes overstates free will’s powers, and dared to say we must first choose goods, then God brings what is his (Hom. 12 on Hebrews), and that divine mercy always seeks the worthy (Hom. 11 on 2 Corinthians)—yet elsewhere he shuts out good works and preaches grace alone. In short: when the Orthodox Fathers say grace is given to those disposing and preparing themselves for grace by labor, good desires, and faith’s beginning, they mean only that from exciting, inspiring grace men are carried—by belief’s affection and conversion’s desire—on to the grace of justification and fuller sanctification.
sections.latin: Chrysostomus, qui aliquando modum excedit in liberi arbitrii viribus exaggerandis, quique ausus est dicere, Nos primum bona eligere oportere, et tunc Deum adferre quae sua sunt, Hom. 12. in Epist. ad Hebr., Divinam misericordiam dignos semper conquirere, Hom. 11. in Epist. 2. ad Corinth., idem tamen alibi bona opera excludit, et solam gratiam depredicat. Ut paucis absolvam, quando Orthodoxi Patres gratiam dari dicunt disponentibus et praeparantibus se ad gratiam per laborem, per bona desideria, per fidei initium, non aliud velle putandi sunt, quam quod ex gratia excitante et inspirante hominibus credulitatis affectum et conversionis desiderium, ad gratiam justificationis et uberioris sanctificationis provehantur.

sections.title: Cap. X Ultimum: if Fathers teach God foresaw the faith of those destined to life, they mean merits he himself would work by predestinating grace — Aug. De praedest. sanct. 10
english: So too when they teach that God foresaw the faith and obedience of those he destined to life, and passed by those he foresaw would be unbelieving and disobedient, they hold that God foresaw in anyone no good merits but those he himself would work in that person by predestinating grace. For by predestination God foresaw what he himself would do—as Augustine truly says (De praedestinatione sanctorum 10).
sections.latin: Sic etiam si quando doceant Deum praescire fidem et obedientiam eorum quos ad vitam destinavit, atque praeteriisse illos quos praevidit infideles et immorigeros futuros, non alia bona merita in quoquam praescisse Deum arbitrantur quam ea quae ipse in eodem per gratiam praedestinationis fuerat facturus. Praedestinatione quippe Deus ea praescivit quae fuerat ipse facturus, ut vere Augustinus, De praedest. sanctor. cap. 10.

sections.title: Cap. X Ultimum ratio: after these premises, Augustine’s Pauline absolute election is proved by a triple cord of three Orthodox axioms outside doubt
english: These premises tasted, we come to our argument: from what catholic consent established, we will show that Augustine’s sentence—also rightly called Pauline—on absolute election and preterition can be proved most firmly and openly. Our reason will be like a triple cord twisted from three Orthodox sentences, all beyond the cast of doubt; granted them, election and non-election or reprobation will be shown to have flowed from God’s absolute good pleasure, not from men’s prior, foreseen, opposite acts. If I am a little long in unfolding this, pardon—it is of highest moment for judging the controversy.
sections.latin: Hisce jam praelibatis ad argumentum nostrum veniemus: In quo ex iis quae communi Catholicorum consensu fuerunt stabilita, ostendemus Augustini sententiam, quam et Paulinam vocare licet, de absoluta electione et praeteritione, posse firmissime et apertissime demonstrari. Ratio autem haec nostra erit instar triplicis funiculi ex tribus constituta et complicata Orthodoxorum sententiis, quae omnes extra dubitationis aleam positae sunt, quibusque concessis, electio et non-electio sive reprobatio ex Dei absoluto beneplacito, non ex hominum praecedaneis, praevisis atque oppositis actibus, fluxisse evincetur. Si paulo prolixior fuero in hisce edisserendis, ignoscite. Sunt maximi momenti ad controversiae hujus dijudicationem.

sections.title: Cap. X Ultimum Major: who hold special efficacious grace prepared for some not others from mere good pleasure hold absolute election — and anti-Pelagian catholics held those three axioms with Augustine
english: So our reason stands: Those who preach and press a special efficacious grace that not only lights the mind, stirs the affections, and knocks the will so that by its help one can believe, repent, and persevere if he wills, but by whose efficacy he always does will—the will healed, even a new will created, faith and charity breathed in, perseverance given; who confess such grace prepared and given by God to some, to others neither prepared nor given; and who teach that God decreed and gave that special grace to some from mere good pleasure, not from prior regard to diverse merits and demerits or any contrary human acts, and to others neither decreed nor gave it—those who hold these three do not hang predestination and preterition or reprobation on foresight of men’s good and evil workings, but on the mere will of God who has mercy on whom he wills and withholds mercy from whom he wills not. But the catholics who opposed Pelagians and Semipelagians defended these three axioms no less than Augustine. Therefore they set absolute election and preterition, not hanging on foresight of men’s faith and unbelief, or obedience and stubbornness.
sections.latin: Sic igitur se habet haec ratio nostra: Qui gratiam quandam specialem et efficacem depredicant urgentque, qua non solummodo illuminatur mens, excitantur affectus, pulsatur voluntas, ut quis ejus beneficio possit credere, poenitere, perseverare, si ipse velit, sed cujus efficacitate semper fiat ut velit; sanata, imo creata in homine nova voluntate, inspirata eidem fide et charitate, ac donata perseverantia; quique hanc talem et tam efficacem gratiam quibusdam a Deo praeparatam et datam agnoscunt, aliis nec praeparatam nec datam; denique, qui Deum eandem specialem gratiam ex mero suo beneplacito, et non ex antecedaneo intuitu ad diversa merita et demerita, sive ad quoslibet hominum actus contrarios, quibusdam donandam decrevisse et donasse docent, aliis nec decrevisse donandam nec donasse; qui, inquam, haec tria tenent, illi praedestinationem et praeteritionem sive reprobationem non ex praevisis hominum operationibus bonis malisque suspendunt, sed ex mera Dei voluntate miserentis cujus vult, et cujus non vult non miserentis: At Catholici illi qui Pelagianis et Semipelagianis sese opposuerunt, non minus quam ipse Augustinus haec tria axiomata propugnarunt: Ergo electionem et praeteritionem absolutam, et minime ex praevisa hominum fide et infidelitate, sive obedientia et contumacia pendulam statuerunt.
